schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole chapter as the Chronicler's swift march over the last four kings; Ellicott notes Jehoahaz (Shallum) was not the firstborn (1 Chron. 3:15) and agrees with 2 Kings 23:30.
Clarke fixes the moment: Necho pressed on toward Carchemish, and while Josiah lay dying the people crowned his son without the conqueror's leave.
Henry reads the ruin coming on by degrees as God's patience — no pleasure in the death of sinners — while Jehoahaz, doing evil, saw his joy but for a moment.

themes: the Chronicler's swift record of the last kings

schools.summary: Keil marks the historian's terseness — age and a brief verdict only; Ellicott notes the queen-mother Hamutal, named in 2 Kings 23:31, is dropped by the Chronicler.
Henry observes the evil-verdict of 2 Kings 23:32 is passed over here, the three-month reign itself standing as the sentence.
Clarke reads the deposition as naked supremacy: Judah now tributary, Jehoahaz dethroned for being crowned without Necho's consent.
Ellicott renders 'removed him,' weighs the LXX/Kings reading of Riblah in Hamath against the Hebrew, and glosses the fine as 'fined the land.'
Henry notes the fine fell on the whole land — the people paid for crowning Jehoahaz.

Ellicott sees the renaming as an act of dominion and notes Kings' addition that Jehoahaz died in Egypt (cf. Jer. 22:10-12); Keil confirms the installation of Eliakim/Jehoiakim and the exile of Jehoahaz.
Henry: the king of Egypt gave what king and what name he pleased, marking Jehoiakim as his own by the imposed name.
Clarke folds the episode into the chapter's survey, Jehoiakim to reign wickedly eleven years.
Ellicott sketches Nebuchadnezzar's rise and inscriptions and rebuts Thenius on the deportation; Keil confirms the stock verdict and reads 'to carry him' as intention, not act.
Clarke marks Jehoiakim as the king who cast off the fear of God and hastened the captivity.

debates.question: Was Jehoiakim actually carried alive to Babylon?

sides.position: No — Nebuchadnezzar left him to reign as a vassal after Carchemish; the text records only the intention 'to carry him'
The chronicler deliberately depicted a live deportation to leave scope for Jeremiah's prophecy

outliers.note: Charges the chronicler with representing Jehoiakim as carried alive to Babylon; Ellicott dismisses it as subjective prejudice, not historical ground.

schools.summary: Keil dates the first campaign to Jehoiakim's fourth year (c. 606 B.C.), the start of the seventy years, and insists the deportation was intended, not executed — Jehoiakim left to reign as vassal.
Henry: Nebuchadnezzar bound him meaning to carry him off, but changed his mind or death released him first.
Clarke, citing Ussher, reckons the seventy years' captivity from this subjection, Jehoiakim tributary three years more.
Keil records the vessels carried to a Babylonian temple; Ellicott (with Daniel 1:2) names it the temple of Bel-Merodach, a wonder of the world to Herodotus.
Henry draws the retributive symmetry: idols brought into God's house are repaid by the vessels carried to the gods of the nations, and traces them to Belshazzar's doom (Dan. 5:3).
Ellicott glosses the 'abominations' as idolatry and tyranny (Jer. 22:13-19) and 'that which was found in him' as general character; notes the LXX/Thenius 'garden of Uzza' burial.
Wesley reads 'that which was found in him' of the secret crime of rebellion, later disclosed.
Henry allows either treachery toward Babylon or, per Jewish writers, private idolatrous marks on his body (cf. Lev. 19:28).

debates.question: What is 'that which was found in him'?

sides.position: His general character and conduct — idolatry and tyranny
The secret crime of rebellion against Babylon, afterward disclosed
Private idolatrous marks or cuttings found on his dead body

outliers.note: Insists the LXX's 'buried in the garden of Uzza' stood in the original but was suppressed because it conflicts with Jeremiah's prophecy of an ass's burial (Jer. 22:18-19); Ellicott finds that very conflict the tell of his motive.

schools.summary: Keil calls 'eight' a clear orthographic error for eighteen; Ellicott clinches it by the yod dropped and by Ezekiel's charge that Jehoiachin 'devoured men' — no boy of eight.
Clarke refers the reader to his notes on 2 Kings 24.
Henry takes 'eight' for a transcriber's slip for eighteen, unless the boy shared rule at eight.

debates.question: Is 'eight years old' correct, or an error for 'eighteen'?

sides.position: A scribal error; eighteen is right (the dropped yod; Ezekiel's charge fits a grown man)
'Eight' is the original reading; the eighteen of Kings is the corruption

themes: an evil grown man, not a child

schools.summary: Ellicott glosses 'return of the year' as spring and corrects 'brother' to 'uncle/kinsman' (Zedekiah a son of Josiah); Keil carries the notice into Zedekiah's doomed reign.
Wesley agrees Zedekiah was 'largely' called brother but was really the uncle; Clarke supplies the renaming of Mattaniah to Zedekiah (2 Kings 24:17).
Henry frames the exile as Abraham's seed returning to the Chaldea he was called from — the covenant forfeited — and lays Zedekiah's ruin to his refusal to humble himself before Jeremiah.
Ellicott ties the data to 2 Kings 24:18 (Hamutal, mother also of Jehoahaz) and names the two sins; Keil sees Zedekiah filling up the measure of sin by defying prophet and oath.
Keil sets the refusal to humble himself before Jeremiah first among Zedekiah's sins, running on into the stiffened neck of v.13.
Henry: because the king would not be a servant to God he was made a slave to his enemies — God humbles those who will not humble themselves (Jer. 1:10).
Clarke laments the whole line of infatuated kings, deputies to God who sinned till there was no remedy.
Ellicott grounds the oath in Ezekiel 17:11-21 ('mine oath that he hath despised'), traces the hardening idioms, and draws Zedekiah as a timorous man ruled by his pro-Egypt princes.
Wesley: the oath by the true God made Zedekiah's rebellion perjury and a horrid contempt of God.
Henry: an oath even to a heathen enemy is sacred; to falsify it is to meet the God to whom vengeance belongs (Ezek. 17:18).

themes: a weak man who hardens himself

schools.summary: Ellicott renders 'the princes... committed manifold unfaithfulness,' tying the temple-idolatry to Ezekiel 8; Keil confirms the reading and reports Bertheau's demur.
Gill: the chief priests, who should have taught pure worship, were the ringleaders of idolatry, and every rank was corrupted with them.
Henry: that place is not far from ruin in which religion is already ruined — the guardians of the sanctuary led the way in.

debates.question: Does the charge of idolatry fall on this last generation's priests and princes, or on the earlier guilt of the whole people?

sides.position: On the priests and people of Zedekiah's own hour, who defiled the temple
Rather on the whole people's earlier guilt, especially in Manasseh's day

schools.summary: Ellicott reads 'rising up betimes and sending' as constant and earnest (Jer. 25:3-4), 'had compassion' as 'spared,' and 'dwelling place' as the temple (Mâʻôn); Keil sets it in the passage's rhetorical build.
Gill names the succession of prophets from Ahijah and Elijah to Jeremiah and Ezekiel, warning from the first step of the apostasy.
Wesley's image: God sent his prophets early and diligently, as a careful householder rises betimes to set his servants to work.

themes: compassion on people and dwelling place

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the rare verbs 'mocked' and 'misused' (each only here), reads 'no remedy' as 'no healing,' and 'wrath arose' as 'went up' like smoke (Ps. 18:8).
Gill: the very treatment Jeremiah and Ezekiel met — messengers mocked, words despised, prophets misused.
Henry: to abuse God's ministers is to affront God himself ('why persecutest thou me?'); this brought wrath without remedy, for it was sinning against the remedy.
Ellicott hears 'he brought up' answering the wrath that 'went up,' sets the sanctuary-slaughter beside Ezekiel 9, and dates Jerusalem's fall to 588 B.C.
Gill: the Lord himself brought the Chaldean, Zedekiah's rebellion only the occasion.
Wesley: 'Chaldees' — Abraham was called out of Ur of the Chaldees; his seed is carried back, the covenant forfeited.
Henry: they fled to the polluted sanctuary for refuge and found no protection, having cast off the God who had compassion on them.

themes: Ur of the Chaldees and the forfeited covenant

schools.summary: Keil gathers the whole seizure of sacred and royal treasures; Ellicott points to the inventory of 2 Kings 25:13-17 and Jeremiah 27:19, reading 'great and small' as a merism for all.
Gill: these were all that were left, earlier reigns having already carried some off.
Henry: all the vessels and treasures, sacred and secular, seized and brought to Babylon — the glory wholly removed.

themes: the vessels and treasures to Babylon

schools.summary: Keil enumerates the temple burnt, walls pulled down, palaces fired, vessels devoted to destruction; Ellicott confirms from 2 Kings 25:9 / Jer. 39:8 and echoes Isaiah 64:11.
Clarke measures the loss item by item — end of the temple, of the fortified city, of the palaces, the vessels beaten into shapeless masses.
Gill notes plainly that they burnt the house of the LORD.
Henry: see what woeful havoc sin makes — keep that worm from the root of your comforts.
Keil reads the verse as the historian's interpretation of prophecy — servitude until the rise of Persia, fulfilling Jeremiah's seventy years (Jer. 27:7; 25:11; 29:10).
Gill: the survivors carried captive, a poorer remnant left to till the land.
Henry: enslaved by the rivers of Babylon (Ps. 137:1), cured of idolatry there but not of mocking the prophets.

themes: a term set to the sentence

schools.summary: Ellicott unfolds the seventy years (Jer. 25:11-12; 29:10), the land's rest as a debt 'discharged' (Lev. 25; 26:34-35), warning against pressing the number too literally; Keil sees God's word exactly fulfilled.
Gill: the long servitude accomplished Jeremiah's prophecy.
Henry: God made the neglected land keep its sabbaths, yet the desolation lay waiting for the exiles, refusing other owners.

Keil treats the edict as the Chronicler's deliberate close, showing God's word fulfilled; Ellicott notes the near-identity with Ezra 1:1 and the idioms 'stirred up the spirit' and 'made a voice pass.'
Gill: the verses match Ezra's opening — either Ezra wrote both, or a transcriber ran on and broke off abruptly.
Clarke: these verses were likely written by mistake from Ezra, the Chronicle properly closing at v.21.
Henry: they show Jeremiah's prophecy accomplished — the set time to favour Zion come at last, God found true.

debates.question: Are vv.22-23 the Chronicler's own close, or a later addition borrowed from Ezra?

sides.position: A transcriber's/mistaken addition from Ezra; the book properly ends at v.21
The Chronicler's deliberate, comforting close on the fulfilled word

themes: the seam between Chronicles and Ezra

schools.summary: Keil sees the Chronicle ending on the open door of return; Ellicott notes the broken syntax (finished in Ezra 1:3), the royal formula like Darius's, and Cyrus identifying Jehovah with Ormazd, 'the God of heaven.'
Clarke closes on the Targum's 'let the Word of the LORD be his helper,' and on a people the most sinful ever, yet displaying the LORD's power, justice, mercy and long-suffering.
Henry: though the church be cast down it is not cast off — the Israel of God fetched out of Babylon, the dry bones made to live.

outliers.note: Reads Cyrus's 'the LORD God of heaven' as a politic syncretism — the title 'God of heaven' being a name of Ormazd/Ahuramazda, with Cyrus identifying the God of Israel with his own Zoroastrian deity.

themes: cast down but not cast off
